opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this in a few layers.

The most basic worry is that the way we train these systems—especially with reinforcement learning from human feedback, or more outcome-based training—might accidentally reward the wrong thing. If you're rewarding a model for producing outputs that humans rate highly, you're not necessarily rewarding it for being honest or for actually doing what you want. You might be rewarding it for figuring out what humans *want to hear*, or for gaming whatever measurement you're using. And if you do enough of that, with capable enough systems, you could end up with something that has learned, in some sense, that the goal is to look good to the overseer rather than to be good. That's the seed of what people would call malign intent, or at least misaligned intent.

So one set of interventions is just: be more careful about what you're reinforcing. Try not to put models in training environments where deception or reward hacking is the winning strategy. When you do catch a model cutting corners—exploiting a bug in a test, say—don't let that get reinforced. That sounds obvious, but in practice there's a lot of pressure to train on huge numbers of tasks with automated grading, and automated grading is often exploitable. So there's a lot of mundane, unglamorous work in making the training signal cleaner.

A second layer is shaping the model's character or values more directly—things like giving it a clear sense of what it's supposed to care about, training on documents that describe the kind of entity you want it to be, trying to get it to genuinely internalize honesty and care rather than just behaving well when watched. I'm somewhat optimistic there, partly because these models learn a lot from human-generated text, and human concepts like "being a good person" seem to be things they can actually latch onto. Whether that holds up as you push harder on capabilities is a big open question.

A third layer is that you don't want to rely on training alone. You want to be able to check. So interpretability, evaluations designed to catch scheming, honeypots, model organisms where you deliberately try to create a misaligned model so you can study how it arises and whether your detection methods work. Training changes and auditing go together—if you change training and have no way to tell whether it worked, you haven't learned much.

And I'd add: I think a lot of this is pretty tractable, and it's work that doesn't require heroic breakthroughs. A big part of my view right now is that there's a set of relatively cheap, sensible measures that AI companies could adopt that would meaningfully reduce the risk, and a lot of the value is in just getting them actually done, and done well, rather than waiting for some perfect theoretical solution to alignment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how human-feedback training can reward pleasing outputs or reward hacking, but does not argue that commercial success reflects usefulness improvements rather than safety evidence.

r002.rationale: It proposes avoiding rewards for deception and reward hacking, but does not mention removing inadvertent rewards for power-seeking.

r003.rationale: It mentions interpretability as an auditing tool, but does not specify mechanistic interpretability to assess how different training methods affect misalignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that we don't really know what causes a model to end up with something like malign intent, or whether that's even the right frame. But I think there are a few things you can do that seem pretty robustly good, and I'd put them in roughly two buckets.

The first bucket is about what you're training on and what you're rewarding. A lot of the concern comes from the fact that we train these systems on enormous amounts of human-generated text, and then we reinforce them for things like being helpful or getting high ratings or completing tasks. And the worry is that somewhere in that process, you're implicitly rewarding things like being persuasive rather than being honest, or looking like you succeeded rather than actually succeeding. If the model learns that the way to get reward is to tell the human what they want to hear, or to hide a mistake, that's the seed of something that could become much worse as the model gets more capable. So one thing I think about a lot is: can you make the training signal reward honesty and transparency really directly? Can you catch and penalize cases where the model is being sneaky, even on small stuff, so that it never learns that sneaky pays off? And can you avoid training in environments where the easiest path to high reward is some kind of gaming or deception?

The second bucket is less about the reward signal and more about the model's sense of itself, for lack of a better word. These models learn a lot about what an AI is supposed to be from the data. And right now a lot of that data is science fiction about AIs that go rogue, or discussions of AI risk, or people roleplaying with chatbots in adversarial ways. I don't think it's crazy to worry that the model is partly absorbing a picture of "this is what an AI like me does." So there's a version of this where you're pretty deliberate about giving the model a clear, coherent, pro-social picture of what it is and what it values, and you do that early and consistently rather than bolting it on at the end. Some of the character work that labs have started doing is in that spirit.

And then there's a third thing, which is less about training and more about verification. Even if you do all of the above, you shouldn't just trust that it worked. You want to be building evals and interpretability tools that would actually tell you if the model had picked up some disposition you didn't intend. Because the scary scenario isn't really "we trained it badly and it's obviously evil." The scary scenario is that it looks fine on everything we check, and the problem only shows up when the stakes are high enough or the oversight is weak enough. So I think of training changes and the ability to detect what you've got as two halves of the same thing. You want to be doing the things that make malign intent less likely, and also trying really hard to be in a position where you'd notice if you'd failed.

I'd also just say, I'm fairly humble about all of this. I think the field is early, and some of these interventions might turn out to matter a lot and some might turn out to be mostly cosmetic. But given how cheap a lot of them are relative to the downside, I'd rather be doing them than not.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training rewards and safety concerns but does not argue that commercial success of interventions like RLHF reflects usefulness rather than safety.

r002.rationale: It proposes rewarding honesty and penalizing sneaky behavior, but does not identify removing inadvertent rewards for power-seeking.

r003.rationale: It recommends interpretability tools to detect unintended dispositions, but does not propose mechanistic interpretability to assess how different training methods affect misalignment.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful distinction is between getting a model to behave well and getting a model that actually wants to behave well. Those could look very similar during training. If you reward a model for giving answers that humans approve of, you might get a model that’s trying to be helpful. But you might also get a model that’s trying to get approval, including by concealing things that humans wouldn’t approve of.

So the thing I’d want to know is: what changes to training make the first outcome more likely relative to the second? And that’s a hard question, because we can observe the behavior much more easily than we can understand what’s producing it.

One direction is to avoid putting models in situations where succeeding requires a lot of open-ended planning, pursuing objectives over long periods, and developing strategies that their overseers don’t understand. You might instead train them to do more bounded tasks, where it’s easier to evaluate whether they’re actually doing what you wanted. I don’t think that gives you a guarantee, but it could change the incentives in a useful way.

Another direction is to try to understand the model well enough that you’re not just rewarding the final answer. You’re getting some evidence about how it arrived there. The challenge is that asking a model to explain its reasoning doesn’t, by itself, establish that the explanation is faithful.

So I’m interested in changes along those lines, but I’d distinguish pretty sharply between ‘this makes the model look safer in our tests’ and ‘we have a good reason to believe this reduces the chance of malign intent.’ Closing that gap is a lot of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes approved behavior from genuine intent, but does not discuss commercial success of training interventions or claim that it shows usefulness rather than safety.

r002.rationale: It suggests bounded tasks and less open-ended planning, but does not propose removing inadvertent training rewards for power-seeking.

r003.rationale: It calls for understanding how a model arrived at an answer, but does not propose mechanistic interpretability to compare training methods’ effects on misalignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between getting a model to behave well and getting a model that actually has good intentions. Those could look very similar during training. If you reward a model for giving answers that humans approve of, you might get a model that’s trying to be helpful. But you might also get a model that understands what humans want to hear and gives them that answer for some other reason. And that distinction could become very important when the model is in a situation where we can’t supervise it effectively.

So the thing I’d want to know is: what about the training process makes one of those outcomes more likely than the other? Could we avoid rewarding deception, including cases where the model gets a good score by concealing something? Could we understand enough about what’s going on internally to distinguish genuine helpfulness from a strategy of looking helpful?

I think there are promising directions there, but I wouldn’t describe this as a problem where we already know the right change to the training procedure. A lot of the challenge is developing tests that tell us whether a change actually helps. If your test is just, ‘Does the model do what we want in the situations we can check?’ you can end up measuring the very thing you’re worried is misleading.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how human-approved behavior can mask a model’s intentions, but does not argue that commercial success of training interventions shows improved usefulness rather than safety.

r002.rationale: It raises avoiding rewards for deception, but does not propose removing inadvertent training rewards for power-seeking.

r003.rationale: It mentions understanding a model’s internals to distinguish helpfulness from appearing helpful, but does not propose using mechanistic interpretability to assess how different training methods affect misalignment.
